segments.text: What if a tiny piece of space junk hit your spaceship? At that speed, it's a bullet.
Since nineteen fifty-seven, humans have launched thousands of rockets and tens of thousands of satellites.
segments.headline: Since 1957

segments.text: Many are still up there. Dead satellites, old rocket stages, and fragments from explosions and collisions.
segments.headline: Still up there

segments.text: The European Space Agency says about forty-seven thousand objects are regularly tracked in orbit.
And it estimates around one and a half million pieces between one and ten centimeters. Too small to track, big enough to destroy a satellite.
In low orbit, they move at about twenty-eight thousand kilometers per hour. Ten times faster than a bullet.
Even a paint fleck can chip a window. The space station regularly moves out of the way of debris.
segments.headline: Dodging debris

segments.text: Scientists worry about Kessler syndrome: one collision creates fragments that cause more collisions, in a chain reaction.
segments.headline: Kessler syndrome

segments.text: Today new satellites are designed to burn up when they're done, and missions are being tested to grab old junk.
segments.headline: Cleaning up

segments.text: Tomorrow, the biggest and most powerful rocket ever built. Next stop: Starship. Which part surprised you most? Tell me in the comments, and follow for tomorrow's stop.
